title: A Chariot Between Two Armies
story:
Somewhere on the field of Kurukshetra stood hundreds of thousands of armed men, but what Arjuna asked to see was only their faces. He and his four brothers, the Pandavas, had come to fight their cousins the Kauravas — two branches of one royal house at war over a kingdom — and both armies were full of men they loved. Dhritarashtra, father of the Kauravas, sat in his palace and asked Sanjaya, his minister, who could see the distant field as clearly as if he stood on it, what his sons and the Pandavas had done, gathered on the sacred plain for battle. And Sanjaya told him, moment by moment, from the first arraying of the armies.

King Duryodhana walked the lines of his own host with Drona, the master of arms who had taught the princes of both houses how to fight. He pointed out the champions drawn up against him — Yuyudhana, Virata, Drupada, Dhrishtadyumna, the ruler of Kasi, Abhimanyu the young son of Arjuna, the sons of Draupadi — and then named his own: Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Ashwatthaman, Vikarna, Jayadratha, and many more ready to lay down their lives for his sake. "Our army, protected by Bhishma, is not enough," he said, "and theirs, protected by Bhima, is more than enough. Station yourselves at the gates of your divisions and protect Bhishma above all."

Then Bhishma, the old grandsire of both families, gave Duryodhana joy by roaring like a lion and blowing his conch. Instantly conches, drums, cymbals, and horns crashed out together until the noise was one great roar. On the Pandava side, Krishna and Arjuna, standing on a great chariot yoked with white horses, blew their celestial conches — Krishna blew Panchajanya, Arjuna blew Devadatta. Bhima of the terrible strength blew his huge conch Paundra; Yudhishthira blew Anantavijaya; the twins Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughosha and Manipushpaka. Then the rulers of the Pandava host — the king of Kasi, Sikhandin, Virata, the unvanquished Satyaki, Drupada, the sons of Draupadi, and Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra — blew theirs in turn, until the sky rang with the sound and it struck at the hearts of the Kauravas.

Then Arjuna, whose banner bore an ape, raised his bow as the first arrows were about to fly, and spoke to Krishna. "Set my chariot between the two armies," he said, "so that I may look at these men who stand here ready to fight — the men I must meet in this war. I want to see the faces of those who have come to battle for Duryodhana, the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra."

Krishna drove the great chariot out between the two armies, where Bhishma and Drona and every king on the field could see them, and said: "Look, Arjuna — these Kurus, gathered before you."

And there, between the two hosts, Arjuna saw them all: standing on both sides were his grandfathers and his grandsons, his friends and his well-wishers, his father-in-law and his teachers, the men who had raised him, his uncles and his brothers-in-law, his cousins, the boys he had grown up beside. And as he looked, something in him gave way. "Seeing these kinsmen before me, Krishna," he began, and his voice failed. His limbs went weak, his mouth went dry, his body trembled, and his hair stood on end; the great bow Gandiva slipped from his hand. "I do not want victory, Krishna," he said at last, "or a kingdom, or pleasures. Of what use is a kingdom, or joy, or life itself, when the people for whose sake we wanted them stand here against us, ready to give up their lives and their wealth? I will not kill these men, even if they kill me — not for the rule of the three worlds, and far less for this earth."

The chariot stood between the armies, the white horses still. The conches were silent and the banners hung quiet while the finest archer of his age looked at the men he loved and found he could not fight them. And Sanjaya's voice, telling it all to the blind king, fell silent too — for the charioteer had not yet spoken.
reflection: Krishna does not drive the chariot where Arjuna can admire the spectacle; he drives it where Arjuna must see that both armies are his family. The survey before battle is no scouting mission — it is the moment the war becomes unbearable, and every word of the Gita will grow out of that unbearable sight.
next_story_tease: In that moment of pity, Arjuna would set down his bow and refuse the war.
hero_scene: Krishna drives the white-steeded chariot between the two vast armies at Kurukshetra, in full view of Bhishma, Drona and all the kings, while Arjuna looks out at the faces of his kinsmen on both sides.
